prompt.context: Our client, Alpha Software, provides technology software to pharmacies. Alpha's product is a highly customizable inventory tracking system. Because of the necessary customization, the time from sale to delivery is on average 12 months. Alpha is considering buying a competitor, Bravo Software. Bravo also sells an inventory tracking product to pharmacies; however its product is less customizable. The average time from sale to delivery is 3 months.
prompt.question: Should Alpha buy Bravo?

clarifying_info.a: 1. A salesperson sells the software to a pharmacy. 2. The customization team customizes the product and delivers it to the client. 3. The service team handles customer service requests and coordinates maintenance.

clarifying_info.q: What are Alpha's and Bravo's revenues?

exhibits.title: Cost Comparisons for Alpha and Bravo
exhibits.shows: A table listing annual costs (in millions) for Alpha and Bravo across six cost center categories.

exhibits.title: Cost Comparisons for Combined Alpha and Bravo
exhibits.shows: A table listing the expected percentage cost decrease and rationale for each cost center of the merged company. A harder version (exhibit_p127.png / exhibit_p129.png) also shows the resulting dollar amounts after the reduction.

data.Advertising & Marketing: 50% decrease — Market both products in current channels
data.Customization: 15% decrease — Minimal impact, product customization requires different skills
data.Overhead: 60% decrease — Office and insurance costs will decrease

framework: Use an M&A framework: evaluate strategic rationale, financials (revenue, cost synergies, profit margin), valuation, and risks/integration
Strategic rationale: Does Bravo complement Alpha? Consider product portfolio (less customizable = faster delivery = different customer segment), market positioning, and competitive dynamics
Financial analysis: Calculate and compare profit margins for Alpha and Bravo individually; then project the merged entity's profit margin after synergies
Cost synergy analysis: Identify each cost center, estimate consolidation savings, and calculate merged-company total costs
Valuation: Determine what price Alpha should pay using comparables, NPV/DCF, or EBITDA multiples
Risks and integration: Human capital retention, technology integration, customer disruption during transition, competitor response

questions.prompt: What are the cost centers for Alpha and Bravo, and which can be consolidated after a merger?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate breaks labor out by function rather than treating it as one line item, because consolidation impacts each function differently. Key cost centers: Executive/Legal/HR, Advertising & Marketing, Sales, Customization team, Customer Service & Maintenance, Overhead (office, insurance). Production/distribution of software is minimal and can be disregarded.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the profit margin for Alpha and Bravo individually. What do you observe?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute (Revenue - Total Costs) / Revenue for each company. Bravo's higher margin signals better cost control and supports the acquisition rationale.

math.setup: Alpha Profit Margin = (Revenue - Total Costs) / Revenue; Bravo Profit Margin = (Revenue - Total Costs) / Revenue. Total Costs = sum of all six cost center lines.
steps: Observation: Bravo has a higher profit margin (40% vs 33%), indicating better cost discipline — a positive signal for acquisition.

questions.prompt: After reviewing the cost centers, what amount of savings can the merged Alpha and Bravo company expect for each cost center? Justify your reasoning.
questions.guidance: There is no single correct numerical answer for the estimates; the interviewer looks for logical reasoning. Expected reasoning: Executive/Legal/HR can be cut ~35% (duplicative leadership); Advertising & Marketing ~50% (shared channels); Sales ~10% (serve different clients, minimal overlap); Customization ~15% (different skill sets needed, limited overlap); Customer Service ~35% (similar skills, can consolidate); Overhead ~60% (reduce office space and insurance). A strong candidate hypothesizes each reduction before seeing Exhibit 2.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2 (with amounts), calculate the merged company's total costs, combined revenue, and profit margin.
questions.guidance: Candidate should apply the percentage reductions to the sum of Alpha + Bravo costs for each line, sum to get merged total costs, combine revenues, then compute margin. A strong candidate does this unprompted after receiving Exhibit 2.

math.setup: For each cost center: Merged cost = (Alpha cost + Bravo cost) × (1 - % decrease). Combined revenue = Alpha revenue + Bravo revenue. Merged margin = (Combined revenue - Merged total costs) / Combined revenue.
math.answer: Merged total costs ≈ $350M; Combined revenue = $800M; Merged profit margin ≈ 55%

questions.prompt: If Alpha were to move forward with the purchase, how would you determine what price to pay for Bravo?
questions.guidance: Candidate does not need to compute a specific number. Should suggest: (1) Comparable transactions / precedent M&A multiples; (2) NPV/DCF using projected future cash flows; (3) EBITDA multiple — note the multiple should be LOW (10-20x) because pharmaceutical software is a low-growth industry, not a high-growth tech sector (60-70x would be inappropriate). Should also acknowledge Alpha's current debt load and financing capacity, and flag integration considerations (human capital, technology integration).

brainstorming.prompt: What additional considerations beyond profit margin and financing should Alpha evaluate before proceeding with the acquisition?

categories.name: Competitive response
ideas: Competitors may target both Alpha and Bravo's existing customers during the merger transition, risking revenue loss
Rivals could rush to acquire other small pharmacy software vendors to block Alpha

categories.name: Revenue synergies and risks
ideas: Cross-sell Alpha's customizable product to Bravo's customer base and vice versa
Risk of customer attrition if service quality drops during integration
Combined revenue may be less than sum of parts if customers churn

categories.name: Human capital
ideas: Key employees (customization, customer service) may leave post-acquisition
Cultural integration between the two organizations
Retention packages and change-management planning needed

categories.name: Technology integration
ideas: Two different software platforms may require significant engineering work to integrate or maintain
Potential technical debt from Bravo's less customizable product

categories.name: Regulatory and legal
ideas: Pharmacy software may face healthcare data regulations (HIPAA, etc.)
Antitrust review if combined market share is significant

recommendation: Alpha should acquire Bravo, assuming the price is right
Bravo's 40% profit margin exceeds Alpha's 33%, indicating strong cost discipline that benefits the merged entity
Post-merger cost consolidation across six cost centers can lift the combined profit margin to approximately 55%, a significant improvement over either standalone business

The product portfolios are complementary: Alpha's highly customizable (12-month) offering and Bravo's faster (3-month) less customizable offering can serve different pharmacy customer segments, broadening the total addressable market
risks: Revenue synergies are uncertain; customer attrition during transition could reduce combined revenue below the assumed $800M
Competitor targeting of both customer bases during the integration window
Human capital and technology integration challenges could erode projected cost savings
Financing cost and current debt load may constrain the price Alpha can pay
next_steps: Determine a fair valuation using comparable transactions and an EBITDA multiple appropriate for low-growth pharmaceutical software (10-20x)
Assess Alpha's financing capacity and current debt
Develop a detailed integration plan covering HR consolidation, technology roadmap, and customer retention strategy
Model downside revenue scenarios (e.g., 5-10% customer attrition) to stress-test the deal economics
